# Support agent TMS access

## Problem Statement

The kick-off transcript named three options for how a customer's identity reaches the TMS, and the mechanism first imagined was each user forwarding their own TMS token. The delivered API removes two of the three options. It authenticates with one global `x-api-key` header and has no user login and no per-user credential, so a customer cannot present a TMS credential they do not have (Option A), and re:cinq cannot exchange or hold one that does not exist (Option B). Option C, a server-held key with the boundary enforced in our own code, is the only option the published API supports.

Identity to us is a separate question, and who signs the customer in is not confirmed yet (RD-5). Whichever provider does, the authenticated identity names a u…

# ADR-001: TMS authentication model

## Context

### Clerk org roles

OLT's customers create their own portal users with different roles (kick-off 2026-08-17). The TMS key is company-scoped, not user-scoped, so a user's role cannot narrow what the TMS returns — the key is the same for every user in the company. Role-based narrowing of results must happen in the support agent's own code if required. This pilot is read-only booking questions; no further narrowing is applied in the PoC.

## Option A — rejected

Each portal user presents their own TMS credential to Otto, which forwards it on every call.

**Rejected because:** The published OLT TMS has no user-level authentication and no login endpoint (`api/README.md`, `api/tms-openapi.json`). A user credential to forward does not exist. The o…

## Why

Kristian's one non-negotiable requirement is that customers "can only speak to their specific bookings, not other customers' bookings." The mechanism originally imagined for this - each user forwarding their own TMS token - doesn't exist: the delivered API authenticates with a single server-held `x-api-key` and has no per-user credential at all. Identity instead comes from our own login, reused from CFOAgent: Clerk authenticates the user, and the Clerk organisation is the customer company, carrying the TMS `customerNumber`. ## Why

Kristian's one non-negotiable requirement for this agent is a boundary: customers "can only speak to their specific bookings, not other customers' bookings." How that boundary is enforced is undecided, and it sets the call signature of every TMS tool and what `auth.ws` validates. The transcript named three options for how a customer's identity reaches the TMS; the delivered API removes two of them outright. It authenticates with one global `x-api-key` header and has no user login and no per-user credential at all, so a customer cannot present a TMS credential they don't have, and re:cinq cannot exchange one that doesn't exist. # ADR-001: TMS authentication model

## Decision

The test that proves customer B's booking id returns an authorization error rather than data:
`apps/api/test/bookingStatusPaths.test.ts` — `shows $reference paid for by $payer and booked by $orderer: $shown` (shown=false when neither payer nor orderer matches the resolver's customer) and `answers customer 20002's shipment exactly as a reference that exists for nobody`.

The kick-off transcript named three options for how a customer's identity reaches the TMS. The delivered OLT TMS External API removes two of them. It authenticates with a single `x-api-key` header on every request; there is no login endpoint, no OAuth flow and no per-user credential. # Support agent TMS access

This feature decides and enforces which customer a TMS call may ask about. The delivered TMS API authenticates with one global, server-held `x-api-key` and has no user login, so the boundary between customers is ours to enforce, not the TMS's. A decision record, `adrs/ADR-001-tms-authentication.md`, accepts that model (Option C), rejects the two alternatives with reasons, and settles the mechanics it leaves open. A scope resolver in `apps/api/src/tools/toolAuth.ts` then derives the `customerNumber` from the authenticated customer company, never from the model and never from the request, and every tool reaches the TMS client through it. Browser headers stop at the resolver, and a missing credential becomes a tool result rather than a crash.

It has no user login, no login endpoint, no OAuth flow and no per-user credential. Forwarding each user's own TMS token (Option A) is therefore impossible, because customers have no TMS credential to present. Exchanging or holding a per-user credential (Option B) is impossible too, because re:cinq can't exchange or hold one that doesn't exist. Option C, a server-held key with the customer boundary enforced in Otto's own code, is the only option the published API supports (ADR-001). The key is company-scoped, not user-scoped, so it can't narrow results by user role. The requirement that customers can only see their own bookings is enforced by Otto instead. Clerk authenticates the user, and the Clerk organisation maps to the TMS `customerNumber`. A scope resolver (`apps/api/src/tools/toolAuth.ts`) derives that `customerNumber` from the authenticated company, never from the model or the request.
